Empirical Research Plan: Pass-Through of Maternity-Coverage Mandates to Wages, Hours, and Employment  

-------------------------------------------------
## 1. Identification Strategy  

Primary design: Difference-in-Differences with a Triple Difference (DDD) extension, supplemented by an event-study.  

Why it fits:

• The mandates were enacted by clearly dated, exogenous state and federal laws.  
• We observe treated and untreated states both before and after the laws.  
• The mandate raises costs only for a subset of workers (women of child-bearing age and, to a lesser extent, their husbands).  
• A DDD contrasts (i) time, (ii) state, and (iii) demographic exposure, thereby purging common shocks and state-specific trends that might bias a simple DiD.  
• An event-study (leads/lags relative to mandate date) allows visual/ statistical checks of the parallel-trends assumption.

-------------------------------------------------
## 2. Treatment and Control  

1. Treatment variable  
   Mandate_st × Post_t × Exposed_i  
   • Mandate_st = 1 for IL, NJ, NY from effective date onward (state DiD); later = 1 nationwide after October 1978 when analysing the federal law.  
   • Post_t = 1 for survey years after the effective date (1977–78 for state laws; 1980–81 for PDA analysis).  
   • Exposed_i = 1 if individual i is in the demographic group with high expected maternity costs:  
        – Women aged 20–40, or  
        – Married men whose spouses are aged 20–40 and whose job provides dependent coverage.  

2. Control group / counterfactual  
   • Spatial: Neighbouring non-adopting states (OH, IN, CT, MA, NC) in the same years.  
   • Demographic: “Non-exposed” workers in the same states—e.g., women 45–55, men 20–40 without a spouse 20–40—provide an additional layer for the triple difference.  

3. Timing / event date  
   • State laws: IL 7/1/1976, NJ 1/1/1977, NY 1/1/1977.  
   • Federal Pregnancy Discrimination Act: 10/31/1978 (effective for plan years starting after that date).  

4. Running variable & cutoff  
   Not applicable; we are not using an RDD.

-------------------------------------------------
## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of mandates, wages/hours/employment of exposed workers in treated states would have evolved like those of (i) exposed workers in control states and (ii) non-exposed workers inside the same states.  
   Plausibility: Treated and control states are contiguous, share labour-market trends, and no other contemporaneous insurance mandates singled out young women.  

A2. No spillovers or anticipation: Firms did not change wages in advance, and workers did not migrate across state lines in response to the pending law.  
   Plausibility: Mandates were passed and implemented quickly; migration costs are high relative to the small expected wage change.  

A3. Stable composition: The demographic makeup of treated vs. control groups is not differentially changing for unrelated reasons.  
   Plausibility: Short pre/post window (≈3 years) limits demographic drift; CPS weighting adjusts for observable composition.  

-------------------------------------------------
## 4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations  

T1. Differential pre-trends  
   – Test: Include event-study leads. If coefficients on leads are ≈0, pre-trends unlikely.  
   – Fix: State-specific linear or quadratic trends as robustness; discard states with visible diverging trends.  

T2. Concurrent state policies (e.g., minimum-wage hikes, union shocks)  
   – Control: Add state-year covariates (unemployment rate, minimum wage) and industry-by-year fixed effects.  
   – Placebo: Re-estimate on older women (45–55) who should not be cost-affected; any significant effect would hint at policy confounding.  

T3. Selective insurance coverage (exposed workers may differ in unobserved ways)  
   – Use information from the Medical Care Expenditure Survey to instrument for probability of being insured in a two-stage “stacked” regression, or, simpler, restrict the main sample to private-sector, full-time workers (highest likelihood of coverage).  
   – Show robustness to including all workers vs. insured-likely subsample.  

-------------------------------------------------
## 5. R Code Outline  

```r
############################################################
# 0. Packages
############################################################
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dim. fixed effects
library(modelsummary)

############################################################
# 1. Load CPS-derived data (already harmonised to one CSV)
############################################################
cps <- read_csv("cps_stack_1974_1982.csv")  # your harmonised file

############################################################
# 2. Variable construction
############################################################
cps <- cps %>% 
  mutate(
    year        = survey_year,
    treated_st  = state %in% c("IL","NJ","NY"),
    post_state  = (treated_st & year >= 1977),                 # state-law post
    post_fed    = (year >= 1980),                              # PDA post
    age_grp     = case_when(age >= 20 & age <= 40 ~ "20_40",
                            age >= 45 & age <= 55 ~ "45_55",
                            TRUE ~ "other"),
    exposed     = if_else(sex=="Female" & age_grp=="20_40",1,0),
    ln_wage     = log(hourly_wage_1978usd),
    weight      = cps_weight
  )

############################################################
# 3. Main DDD for state laws, young women vs older women
############################################################
ddd_state <- feols(
  ln_wage ~ post_state*treated_st*exposed + 
            sex + race + educ + union +
            fe(state) + fe(year),
  data = cps %>% filter(year %in% c(1974,1975,1977,1978)),
  weights = ~weight,
  cluster = ~state
)
etable(ddd_state)

############################################################
# 4. Event-study (young women only) ------------------------
############################################################
cps_es <- cps %>%
  filter(sex=="Female", age_grp=="20_40") %>%
  mutate(event_time = year - 1976)  # 0 = first treated year

es <- feols(ln_wage ~ i(event_time, treated_st, ref = -1) + 
              fe(state) + fe(year), 
            data = cps_es, cluster = ~state, weights = ~weight)
iplot(es)        # visual pre-trend check

############################################################
# 5. Robustness: placebo on older women (should be 0) ------
############################################################
placebo <- feols(
  ln_wage ~ post_state*treated_st, 
  data = cps %>% filter(sex=="Female", age_grp=="45_55"),
  fe = c("state","year"), cluster = "state", weights = ~weight)
etable(placebo)
```

-------------------------------------------------
## 6. Expected Results  

Economic incidence theory predicts most of the cost is shifted to workers whose labour-supply elasticity exceeds the firms’ demand elasticity for that group. Women 20–40 likely have relatively inelastic labour supply to their current employers (job-match, location, amenities), so:

• Wages: 50–100 percent passthrough ⇒ expect a 0.5–4.0 percent drop in real hourly wages (mean mandate cost ≈1–5 percent of payroll).  
• Hours: small negative or zero (firms may prefer wage adjustment to costly hours cuts).  
• Employment: little effect; mandates are modest relative to total compensation, so separation elasticity should be low.

-------------------------------------------------
## 7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = met, 0 = unsure)  

C1 Parallel pre-trends visually flat in event-study lead coefficients ……………… 1  
C2 No obvious contemporaneous policies in treated vs control states ……………… 0  
C3 Composition stability (age, education, unionisation) ……………………………… 1  
C4 No spillovers/anticipation (checked via leads & migration data) ……………… 1  
C5 Measurement error in outcome & treatment modest (CPS wages, clear law dates) 0  

Total = 3 / 5.  

The design is strong but vigilance is needed on concurrent policies (C2) and potential mis-measurement of actual insurance status (C5).
